entries.e362782abcca4dd4f8231064832eb007e3ceeb0e: <div sID="gen8150" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="2Chr.14" sID="2Chr.14"/> <div eID="gen8150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8151" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8152" type="x-p"/> In this and the two following chapters we have the history of the reign of Asa, a good reign and a long one. In this chapter we have, I. His piety, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.1-2Chr.13.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. His policy, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.6-2Chr.13.8">ver. 6-8</reference>. III. His prosperity, and particularly a glorious victory he obtained over a great army of Ethiopians that came out against him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.9-2Chr.13.15">ver. 9-15</reference>.
entries.a760e137e7d4292aa57d15a94c051767122f1e43: <div eID="gen8152" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8151" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Asa King of Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 955.)</title> <div sID="gen8153" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> So Abijah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David: and Asa his son reigned in his stead. In his days the land was quiet ten years. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Asa did <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> good and right in the eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his God: <hi type="super">3</hi> For he took away the altars of the strange <hi type="italic">gods,</hi> and the high places, and brake down the images, and cut down the groves: <hi type="super">4</hi> And commanded Judah to seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of their fathers, and to do the law and the commandment. <hi type="super">5</hi> Also he took away out of all the cities of Judah the high places and the images: and the kingdom was quiet before him. <hi type="super">6</hi> And he built fenced cities in Judah: for the land had rest, and he had no war in those years; because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had given him rest. <hi type="super">7</hi> Therefore he said unto Judah, Let us build these cities, and make about <hi type="italic">them</hi> walls, and towers, gates, and bars, <hi type="italic">while</hi> the land <hi type="italic">is</hi> yet before us; because we have sought the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God, we have sought <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and he hath given us rest on every side. So they built and prospered. <hi type="super">8</hi> And Asa had an army <hi type="italic">of men</hi> that bare targets and spears, out of Judah three hundred thousand; and out of Benjamin, that bare shields and drew bows, two hundred and fourscore thousand: all these <hi type="italic">were</hi> mighty men of valour. <div eID="gen8153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8154" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Asa's general character (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.2">v. 2</reference>): He did <hi type="italic">that which was good and right in the eyes of the Lord his God.</hi> 1. He aimed at pleasing God, studied to approve himself to him. Happy are those that walk by this rule, to do that which is right, not in their own eyes, or in the eye of the world, but in the eyes of God. 2. He saw God's eye always upon him, and that helped much to keep him to what was good and right. 3. God graciously accepted him in what he did, and approved his conduct as good and right. <div eID="gen8154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8155" type="x-p"/> II. A blessed work of reformation which he set on foot immediately upon his accession to the crown. 1. He removed and abolished idolatry. Since Solomon admitted idolatry, in the latter end of his reign, nothing had been done to suppress it, and so, we presume, it had got ground. Strange gods were worshipped and had their altars, images, and groves; and the temple service, though kept up by the priests (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.10">ch. xiii. 10</reference>), was neglected by many of the people. Asa, as soon as he had power in his hands, made it his business to destroy all those idolatrous altars and images (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.3">v. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.5">5</reference>), they being a great provocation to a jealous God and a great temptation to a careless unthinking people. He hoped by destroying the idols to reform the idolaters, which he aimed at, rather than to ruin them. 2. He revived and established the pure worship of God; and, since the priests did their part in attending God's altars, he obliged the people to do theirs (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">He commanded Judah to seek the Lord God of their fathers,</hi> and not the gods of the heathen, and <hi type="italic">to do the law and the commandments,</hi> that is, to observe all divine institutions, which many had utterly neglected. In doing this, <hi type="italic">the land was quiet before him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.5">v. 5</reference>. Though they were much in love with their idols, and very loth to leave them, yet the convictions of their consciences sided with the commands of Asa, and they could not, for shame, refuse to comply with them. Note, Those that have power in their hands, and will use it vigorously for the suppression of profaneness and the reformation of manners, will not meet with so much difficulty and opposition therein as perhaps they feared. Vice is a sneaking thing, and virtue has reason enough on its side to make <hi type="italic">all iniquity stop her mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.42">Ps. cvii. 42</reference>. <div eID="gen8155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8156" type="x-p"/> III. The tranquillity of his kingdom, after constant alarms of war during the last two reigns: <hi type="italic">In his days the land was quiet ten years</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1">v. 1</reference>), no war with the kingdom of Israel, who did not recover the blow given them in the last reign for a great while. Abijah's victory, which was owing, under God, to his courage and bravery, laid a foundation for Asa's peace, which was the reward of his piety and reformation. Though Abijah had little religion himself, he was instrumental to prepare the way for one that had much. If Abijah had not done what he did to quiet the land, Asa could not have done what he did to reform it; for <hi type="italic">inter arma silent leges</hi>—<hi type="italic">amidst the din of arms the voice of law is unheard.</hi> <div eID="gen8156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8157" type="x-p"/> IV. The prudent improvement he made of that tranquillity: <hi type="italic">The land had rest, for the Lord had given him rest.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">If God give quietness, who then can make trouble?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.34.29">Job xxxiv. 29</reference>. Those have rest indeed to whom God gives rest, peace indeed to whom Christ gives peace, <hi type="italic">not as the world giveth,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.27">John xiv. 27</reference>. Now, 1. Asa takes notice of the rest they had as the gift of God (<hi type="italic">He hath given us rest on every side.</hi> Note, God must be acknowledged with thankfulness in the rest we are blessed with, of body and mind, family and country), and as the reward of the reformation begun: <hi type="italic">Because we have sought the Lord our God, he has given us rest.</hi> Note, As the frowns and rebukes of Providence should be observed for a check to us in an evil way, so the smiles of Providence should be taken notice of for our encouragement in that which is good. See <reference osisRef="Hag.2.18-Hag.2.19">Hag. ii. 18, 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mal.3.10">Mal. iii. 10</reference>. We find by experience that it is good to <hi type="italic">seek the Lord;</hi> it <hi type="italic">gives us rest.</hi> While we pursue the world we meet with nothing but vexation. 2. He consults with his people, by their representatives, how to make a good use of the present gleams of peace they enjoyed, and concludes with them, (1.) That they must not be idle, but busy. Times of rest from war should be employed in work, for we must always find ourselves something to do. In the years when he had no war he said, "Let us build; still let us be doing." When the <hi type="italic">churches had rest</hi> they were <hi type="italic">built up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.9.31">Acts ix. 31</reference>. When the sword is sheathed take up the trowel. (2.) That they must not be secure, but prepare for wars. In times of peace we must be getting ready for trouble, expect it and lay up in store for it. [1.] He fortified his principle cities with <hi type="italic">walls, towers, gates, and bars,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.7">v. 7</reference>. "This let us do," says he, "<hi type="italic">while the land is yet before us,</hi>" that is, "while we have opportunity and advantage for it and have nothing to hinder us." He speaks as if he expected that, some way or other, trouble would arise, when it would be too late to fortify, and when they would wish they had done it. <hi type="italic">So they built and prospered.</hi> [2.] He had a good army ready to bring into the field (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.8">v. 8</reference>), not a standing army, but the militia or trained-bands of the country. Judah and Benjamin were mustered severally; and Benjamin (which not long ago was called <hi type="italic">little Benjamin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.27">Ps. lxviii. 27</reference>) had almost as many soldiers as Judah, came as near as 28 to 30, so strangely had that tribe increased of late. The blessing of God can make a <hi type="italic">little one to become a thousand.</hi> It should seem, these two tribes were differently armed, both offensively and defensively. The men of Judah guarded themselves with targets, the men of Benjamin with shields, the former of which were much larger than the latter, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.16-1Kgs.10.17">1 Kings x. 16, 17</reference>. The men of Judah fought with spears when they closed in with the enemy; the men of Benjamin drew bows, to reach the enemy at a distance. Both did good service, and neither could say to the other, I have <hi type="italic">no need of thee.</hi> Different gifts and employments are for the common good.
entries.fe77069ea4dc41fcfd05131aedd9b1617f76bc27: <div eID="gen8157" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Asa Defeats the Ethiopians. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 945.)</title> <div sID="gen8158" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And there came out against them Zerah the Ethiopian with an host of a thousand thousand, and three hundred chariots; and came unto Mareshah. <hi type="super">10</hi> Then Asa went out against him, and they set the battle in array in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah. <hi type="super">11</hi> And Asa cried unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his God, and said, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">it is</hi> nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> our God; for we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude<hi type="small-caps">. O Lord</hi> , thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> our God; let not man prevail against thee. <hi type="super">12</hi> So the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> smote the Ethiopians before Asa, and before Judah; and the Ethiopians fled. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Asa and the people that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him pursued them unto Gerar: and the Ethiopians were overthrown, that they could not recover themselves; for they were destroyed before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and before his host; and they carried away very much spoil. <hi type="super">14</hi> And they smote all the cities round about Gerar; for the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came upon them: and they spoiled all the cities; for there was exceeding much spoil in them. <hi type="super">15</hi> They smote also the tents of cattle, and carried away sheep and camels in abundance, and returned to Jerusalem. <div eID="gen8158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8159" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Disturbance given to the peace of Asa's kingdom by a formidable army of Ethiopians that invaded them, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.9-2Chr.14.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. Though still they sought God, yet this fear came upon them, that their faith in God might be tried, and that God might have an opportunity of doing great things for them. It was a vast number that the Ethiopians brought against him: 1,000 000 <hi type="italic">men;</hi> and now he found the benefit of having an army ready raised against such a time of need. That provision which we thought needless may soon appear to be of great advantage. <div eID="gen8159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8160" type="x-p"/> II. The application Asa made to God on occasion of the threatening cloud which now hung over his head, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.11">v. 11</reference>. He that sought God in the day of his peace and prosperity could with holy boldness cry to God in the day of his trouble, and call him <hi type="italic">his God.</hi> His prayer is short, but has much in it. 1. He gives to God the glory of his infinite power and sovereignty: <hi type="italic">It is nothing with thee to help</hi> and save by many or few, by those that are mighty or by <hi type="italic">those that have no power.</hi> See <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.6">1 Sam. xiv. 6</reference>. God works in his own strength, not in the strength of instruments (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.13">Ps. xxi. 13</reference>), nay, it is his glory to <hi type="italic">help the weakest</hi> and to <hi type="italic">perfect strength out of the mouth of babes and sucklings.</hi> "We do not say, Lord, take our part, for we have a good army for thee to work by; but, take our part, for without thee we have no power." 2. He takes hold of their covenant-relation to God as theirs. <hi type="italic">O Lord, our God!</hi> and again, "<hi type="italic">Thou art our God,</hi> whom we have chosen and cleave to as ours, and who hast promised to be ours." 3. He pleads their dependence upon God, and the eye they had to him in this expedition. He was well prepared for it, yet trusted not to his preparations; but, "Lord, <hi type="italic">we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude,</hi> by warrant from thee, aiming at thy glory, and trusting to thy strength." 4. He interests God in their cause: "<hi type="italic">Let not man" (mortal man,</hi> so the word is) "<hi type="italic">prevail against thee.</hi> If he prevail against us, it will be said that he prevails against thee, because thou art our God, and we rest on thee and go forth in thy name, which thou hast encouraged us to do. The enemy is a mortal man; make it to appear what an unequal match he is for an immortal God. Lord, maintain thy own honour; <hi type="italic">hallowed by thy name.</hi>" <div eID="gen8160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8161" type="x-p"/> III. The glorious victory God gave him over his enemies. 1. God defeated the enemy, and put their forces into disorder (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord smote the Ethiopians,</hi> smote them with terror, and an unaccountable consternation, so that they fled, and knew neither why nor whither. 2. Asa and his soldiers took the advantage God gave them against the enemy. (1.) They destroyed them. They fell <hi type="italic">before the Lord</hi> (for who can stand before him?) and before his host, either an invisible host of angels that were employed to destroy them or the host of Israel, called <hi type="italic">God's host</hi> because owned by him. (2.) They took the plunder of their camp, <hi type="italic">carried away very much spoil</hi> from the slain and from the baggage. (3.) They <hi type="italic">smote the cities</hi> that were in league with them, to which they fled for shelter, and carried off the spoil of them (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.14">v. 14</reference>); and they were not able to make any resistance, <hi type="italic">for the fear of the Lord came upon them,</hi> that is, a fear which God struck them with to such a degree that they had no heart to withstand the conquerors. (4.) They fetched away the cattle out of the enemy's country, in vast numbers, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.15">v. 15</reference>. Thus the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just.  <chapter eID="2Chr.14"/> <div eID="gen8161" type="x-p"/>

entries.43c2c341e04bf98870745c2ff85adcfff605999e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4007"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <div sID="gen5792" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1-2Chr.14.5">2Ch 14:1-5</reference>. Asa Destroys Idolatry.<div eID="gen5792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5793" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4007"/><hi type="bold">1. In his days the land was quiet ten years--</hi>This long interval of peace was the continued effect of the great battle of Zemaraim (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.11-1Kgs.15.14">1Ki 15:11-14</reference>). <div eID="gen5793" type="x-p"/>
entries.040234800204598cc691aca94a38765bb98f1428: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4008"/><div sID="gen5794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4008"/><hi type="bold">2. Asa did that which was good and right--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.14">1Ki 15:14</reference>). Still his character and life were not free from faults (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.7">2Ch 16:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.12">10, 12</reference>). <div eID="gen5794" type="x-p"/>
entries.24780ab902f57d5b050432a0b74bff0c715866cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4009"/><div sID="gen5795" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4009"/><hi type="bold">3. brake down the images--</hi>of Baal (see on <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.4">2Ch 34:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Le 26:30</reference>).<div eID="gen5795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut down the groves--</hi>rather, "Asherim." <div eID="gen5796" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b4cb9f1a24d12782511a3234d41de3c40c0f19b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4010"/><div sID="gen5797" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4010"/><hi type="bold">5. he took away ... the high places--</hi>that is, those devoted to idolatrous rites.<div eID="gen5797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">took away out of all the cities of Judah the high places and the images--</hi>All public objects and relics of idolatry in Jerusalem and other cities through his kingdom were destroyed; but those high places where God was worshipped under the figure of an ox, as at Beth-el, were allowed to remain (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.14">1Ki 15:14</reference>); so far the reformation was incomplete.<div eID="gen5798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5799" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.6-2Chr.14.8">2Ch 14:6-8</reference>. Having Peace, He Strengthens His Kingdom with Forts and Armies. <div eID="gen5799" type="x-p"/>
entries.27e75be25fadd391a8f790e2c5e705742bd60c3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4011"/><div sID="gen5800" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4011"/><hi type="bold">6. he built fenced cities in Judah--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.22">1Ki 15:22</reference>). <div eID="gen5800" type="x-p"/>
entries.90b38e39708388543a8cf4a952356365036c831c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4012"/><div sID="gen5801" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4012"/><hi type="bold">7. while the land is yet before us--</hi>that is, while we have free and undisputed progress everywhere; no foe is near; but, as this happy time of peace may not last always and the kingdom is but small and weak, let us prepare suitable defenses in case of need. He had also an army of five hundred eighty thousand men. Judah furnished the heavily armed soldiers, and Benjamin the archers. This large number does not mean a body of professional soldiers, but all capable of bearing arms and liable to be called into service.<div eID="gen5801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5802" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.9-2Chr.14.15">2Ch 14:9-15</reference>. He Overcomes Zerah, and Spoils the Ethiopians. <div eID="gen5802" type="x-p"/>
entries.41c714aa947861a6aa446004f2af89694cd0867c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4013"/><div sID="gen5803" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4013"/><hi type="bold">9. there came out against them Zerah the Ethiopian--</hi>This could not have been from Ethiopia south of the cataracts of the Nile, for in the reign of Osorkon I, successor of Shishak, no foreign army would have been allowed a free passage through Egypt. Zerah must, therefore, have been chief of the Cushites, or Ethiopians of Arabia, as they were evidently a nomad horde who had a settlement of tents and cattle in the neighborhood of Gerar.<div eID="gen5803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a thousand thousand, and three hundred chariots--</hi>"Twenty camels employed to carry couriers upon them might have procured that number of men to meet in a short time. As Zerah was the aggressor, he had time to choose when he would summon these men and attack the enemy. Every one of these Cushite shepherds, carrying with them their own provisions of flour and water, as is their invariable custom, might have fought with Asa without eating a loaf of Zerah's bread or drinking a pint of his water" [Bruce, Travels]. <div eID="gen5804" type="x-p"/>
entries.7dce818003aaf594ebbdf87a71869f3aae6f99ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4014"/><div sID="gen5805" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4014"/><hi type="bold">10. Then Asa went out against him, and they set the battle in array ... at Mareshah--</hi>one of the towns which Rehoboam fortified (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.8">2Ch 11:8</reference>), near a great southern pass in the low country of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.44">Jos 15:44</reference>). The engagement between the armies took place in a plain near the town, called "the valley of Zephathah," supposed to be the broad way coming down Beit Jibrin towards Tell Es-Safren [Robinson]. <div eID="gen5805" type="x-p"/>
entries.c54d08af99427e1ead1305b6909b242fd881bc36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4015"/><div sID="gen5806" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4015"/><hi type="bold">11-13. Asa cried unto the Lord his God--</hi>Strong in the confidence that the power of God was able to give the victory equally with few as with many, the pious king marched with a comparatively small force to encounter the formidable host of marauders at his southern frontier. Committing his cause to God, he engaged in the conflict--completely routed the enemy, and succeeded in obtaining, as the reward of his victory, a rich booty in treasure and cattle from the tents of this pastoral horde. <chapter eID="2Chr.14"/>

entries.a8f142cbb7e92f9af632a6f0bf18d759c0500a4e: <div eID="gen14210" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14211" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14212" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14212" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14211" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14213" type="x-p"/> Asa succeeds his father Abijah, reigns piously, and has peace for ten years, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1">2Chr 14:1</reference>. He makes a great reformation in Judah, and builds cities of defense, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.2-2Chr.14.7">2Chr 14:2-7</reference>. His military strength, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.8">2Chr 14:8</reference>. He is attacked by Zerah the Ethiopian, with an immense army; Asa cries to the Lord, attacks the Ethiopians, and gives them a total overthrow, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.9-2Chr.14.12">2Chr 14:9-12</reference>. He takes several of their cities, their cattle, etc., and returns to Jerusalem, laden with spoils, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.13-2Chr.14.15">2Chr 14:13-15</reference>. <div eID="gen14213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14214" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen14214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14215" type="x-p"/> The land was quiet ten years - Calmet thinks these years should be counted from the fifth to the fifteenth of Asa's reign.
entries.f195590926e0091b471f2c6e7b3a967986c3ee75: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen14215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14216" type="x-p"/> Did that which was good - He attended to what the law required relative to the worship of God. He was no idolater, though, morally speaking, he was not exempt from faults, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.14">1Kgs 15:14</reference>. He suppressed idolatry universally, and encouraged the people to worship the true God: see <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.3-2Chr.14.5">2Chr 14:3-5</reference>.
entries.d800b714847457dd2bc8e8f1e89dddb6aaf29928: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen14216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14217" type="x-p"/> Fenced cities - To preserve his territories from invasion, and strengthen the frontiers of his kingdom, see <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.7">2Chr 14:7</reference>.
entries.151823383413d1d1cd2a6698306691a40f7100d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen14217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14218" type="x-p"/> Targets and spears - Probably targets with the dagger in the center, and javelins for distant fight. <div eID="gen14218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14219" type="x-p"/> Bare shields and drew bows - They were not only archers, but had shield and sword for close fight.
entries.ca8977b748258986380f6e14e72208e87f52c164: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen14219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14220" type="x-p"/> Zerah the Ethiopian - Probably of that Ethiopia which lay on the south of Egypt, near to Libya, and therefore the Libyans are joined with them, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.8">2Chr 16:8</reference>. <div eID="gen14220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14221" type="x-p"/> A thousand thousand - If this people had come from any great distance, they could not have had forage for such an immense army.
entries.d003146aa93c0cf226ba554b4f02738549fa9d6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen14221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14222" type="x-p"/> Whether with many - The same sentiment as that uttered by Jonathan, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.6">1Sam 14:6</reference>, when he attacked the garrison of the Philistines. <div eID="gen14222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14223" type="x-p"/> O Lord our God - we rest on thee - "Help us, O Lord our God; because we depend on thy Word, and in the name of thy Word we come against this great host." - Targum.
entries.db7044f9c64f1245b08df50cabaad68aedbc99d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen14223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14224" type="x-p"/> There was - much spoil in them - These cities being on the rear of this vast army, they had laid up much forage in them; and to get this the Jews overthrew the whole.
entries.78f8f071e7b6fbea90905d7ab61fe91b8a28bceb: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen14224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14225" type="x-p"/> Tents of cattle - Those which had carried the baggage of the great army, and which they had left in such places as abounded with pasture. Perhaps sheepfolds, enclosures for camels, mules, etc., may also be intended. The discomfiture was great, because God fought for the people; and the spoil was immense, because the multitude was prodigious, indeed almost incredible, a million of men in one place is almost too much for the mind to conceive, but there may be some mistake in the numerals: it is evident from the whole account that the number was vast and the spoil great.  <chapter eID="2Chr.14"/> <div eID="gen14225" type="x-p"/>

entries.742bfc608b44252c7aa5815361339d19203af490: <div eID="gen6011" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Asa’s Reign - 2 Chronicles 14-16</title> <div sID="gen6012" type="x-p"/> In 1 Kings 15:9-24 it is merely recorded of Asa, that he reigned forty-one years, did that which was right as David did, removed from the land all the idols which his fathers had made, and, although the high places were not removed, was devoted to the Lord during his whole life, and laid up in the temple treasury all that had been consecrated by his father and himself. Then it is related that when Baasha marched against him, and began to fortify Ramah, he induced the Syrian king Benhadad, by sending to him the treasures of the temple and of his palace, to break faith with Baasha, and to make an inroad upon and smite the northern portion of the land; that Baasha was thereby compelled to abandon the building of Ramah, and to fall back to Tirzah, and that thereupon Asa caused the fortifications of Ramah to be pulled down, and the cities Geba and Benjamin and Mizpah to be fortified with the materials; and, finally, it is recorded that Asa in his old age became diseased in his feet, and died. The Chronicle also characterizes Asa as a pious king, who did that which was right, and removed the high places and sun-pillars in the land; but gives, as to other matters, a much more detailed account of his reign of forty-one years. It states that in the first years, as the land had rest, he built fortified cities in Judah, and had an army fit for war (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1-2Chr.14.7">2Ch 14:1-7</reference>); that thereupon he marched against the Cushite Zerah, who was then advancing upon Judah with an innumerable host, prayed for help to the Lord, who then smote the Cushites, so that they fled; and that Asa pursued them to Gerar, and returned with great booty (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.8-2Chr.14.14">2Ch 14:8-14</reference>). Then we learn that the prophet Azariah, the son of Oded, came to meet him, who, pointing to the victory which the Lord had granted them, called upon the king and the people to remain stedfast in their fidelity to the Lord; that Asa thereupon took courage, extirpated all the still remaining idolatrous abominations from the land, and in the fifteenth year of his reign held with the people a great sacrificial feast in Jerusalem, renewed the covenant with the Lord, crushed out all the remains of former idolatry, although the high places were not destroyed, and also deposited in the temple treasury all that had been consecrated by his father and himself (2 Chron 15). Thereafter Baasha’s inroad upon Judah and the alliance with Ben-hadad of Syria are narrated (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.1-2Chr.16.6">2Ch 16:1-6</reference>), as in the book of Kings; but it is also added that the prophet Hanani censured his seeking help from the king of Syria, and was thereupon put into the prison-house by Asa (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.7-2Chr.16.10">2Ch 16:7-10</reference>); and then we have an account of the end of his reign, in which several additions to the account in 1 Kings are communicated (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.11-2Chr.16.14">2Ch 16:11-14</reference>). <div eID="gen6012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6013" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1-2Chr.14.3">2Ch 14:1-3</reference> <hi type="italic">Asa’s efforts for the abolition of idolatry and the establishment of the kingdom</hi>. - <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1">2Ch 14:1</reference>-4. The good and right in God’s eyes which Asa did is further defined in <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.2">2Ch 14:2</reference>-4. He abolished all the objects of the idolatrous worship. The “altars of the strangers” are altars consecrated to foreign gods; from them the בּמות, high places, are distinguished-these latter being illegal places of sacrifice connected with the worship of Jahve (see on 1Ki 15:14). The מצּבוה are the statues or monumental columns consecrated to Baal, and אשׁרים the wooden idols, tree-trunks, or trees, which were consecrated to Astarte (see on 1Ki 14:23 and <reference osisRef="Deut.16.21">Deu 16:21</reference>). Asa at the same time commanded the people to worship Jahve, the God of the fathers, and to follow the law.
entries.dc28e8d7a4209a0b1b2a7bfe87c6c7cbd7a5cadd: <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.4-2Chr.14.6">2Ch 14:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen6013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6014" type="x-p"/> He removed from all the cities of Judah the altars of the high places, and the חמּנים, sun-pillars, pillars or statues consecrated to Baal as sun-god, which were erected near or upon the altars of Baal (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.4">2Ch 34:4</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Lev 26:30</reference>). In consequence of this the kingdom had rest לפניו, before him, i.e., under his oversight (cf. Num 8:22). This ten-years’ quiet (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1">2Ch 14:1</reference>) which God granted him, Asa employed in building fortresses in Judah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.5">2Ch 14:5</reference>). “We will build these cities, and surround them with walls and towers, gates and bolts.” It is not said what the cities were, but they were at any rate others than Geba and Mizpah, which he caused to be built after the war with Baasha (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.6">2Ch 16:6</reference>). “The land is still before us,” i.e., open, free from enemies, so that we may freely move about, and build therein according to our pleasure. For the phraseology, cf. Gen 13:9. The repetition of דּרשׁנוּ, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.6">2Ch 14:6</reference>, is impassioned speech. “They built and had success;” they built with effect, without meeting with any hindrances.
entries.18bdf31e9e4e77e5bf75b9ceba39f99e0553c5eb: <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.7">2Ch 14:7</reference> <div eID="gen6014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6015" type="x-p"/> Asa had also a well-equipped, well-armed army. The men of Judah were armed with a large shield and lance (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.24">1Ch 12:24</reference>), the Benjamites with a small shield and bow (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.40">1Ch 8:40</reference>). The numbers are great; of Judah 300,000, of Benjamin 280,000 men. Since in these numbers the whole population capable of bearing arms is included, 300,000 men does not appear too large for Judah, but 280,000 is a very large number for Benjamin, and is founded probably on an overestimate.
entries.46aa3ca50d8fcda51fc08c855eaa8d9ccfef67fa: <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.8">2Ch 14:8</reference> <hi type="italic">The victory over the Cushite Zerah</hi>. - 2Ch 14:8. “And there went forth against them Zerah.” אליהם for עליהם refers to Asa’s warriors mentioned in 2Ch 14:7. The number of the men in Judah capable of bearing arms is mentioned only to show that Asa set his hope of victory over the innumerable host of the Cushites not on the strength of his army, but on the all-powerful help of the Lord (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.10">2Ch 14:10</reference>). The Cushite זרח is usually identified with the second king of the 22nd (Bubastitic) dynasty, Osorchon I; while Brugsch, <hi type="italic">hist. de l'Eg.</hi> i. p. 298, on the contrary, has raised objections, and holds Zerah to be an Ethiopian and not an Egyptian prince, who in the reign of Takeloth I, about 944 b.c., probably marched through Egypt as a conqueror (cf. G. Rösch in Herz.'s <hi type="italic">Realenc.</hi> xviii. S. 460). The statement as to Zerah’s army, that it numbered 1,000,000 warriors and 300 war-chariots, rests upon a rough estimate, in which 1000 times 1000 expresses the idea of the greatest possible number. The Cushites pressed forward to Mareshah, i.e., Marissa, between Hebron and Ashdod (see on <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.8">2Ch 11:8</reference>).
entries.2c6cf55afff951803cf6748e28748b8d50457210: <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.9">2Ch 14:9</reference> <div eID="gen6015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6016" type="x-p"/> Thither Asa marched to meet them, and drew up his army in battle array in the valley Zephathah, near Mareshah. The valley Zephathah is not, as Robins., <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> <hi type="italic">sub voce</hi>, thinks, to be identified with Tel es Safieh, but must lie nearer Mareshah, to the west or north-west of Marâsch.
entries.eddc30c6a062ec75c2050af91635ebbe26748f49: <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.10">2Ch 14:10</reference> <div eID="gen6016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6017" type="x-p"/> Then he called upon the Lord his God for help. וגו עמּך אין we translate, with Berth., “None is with Thee (on עמּך, cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.6">2Ch 20:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.25">Psa 73:25</reference>) to help between a mighty one and a weak,” i.e., no other than Thou can help in an unequal battle, i.e., help the weaker side; while the Vulg., on the contrary, after the analogy of <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.6">1Sa 14:6</reference>, translates, <hi type="italic">“non est apud te ulla distantia, utrum in paucis auxilieris an in pluribus;”</hi> and the older commentators (Schmidt, Ramb.) give the meaning thus: <hi type="italic">“perinde est tibi potentiori vel imbecilliori opem ferre.”</hi> But in <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.16">1Sa 14:16</reference> the wording is different, so that that passage cannot be a standard for us here. “In Thy name (i.e., trusting in Thy help) are we come against this multitude” (not “have we fallen upon this multitude”). וגו יעצר אל, “Let not a mortal retain strength with Thee” (עצר = כּח עצר,   <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.20">2Ch 13:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.14">1Ch 29:14</reference>), i.e., let not weak men accomplish anything with Thee, show Thy power or omnipotence over weak men.
entries.8c38e43e9e3c4e28fd75a02ad75e3465be87baec: <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.11">2Ch 14:11</reference> <div eID="gen6017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6018" type="x-p"/> God heard this prayer. Jahve drove the Cushites into flight before Asa, <hi type="italic">scil.</hi> by His mighty help.
entries.a67858c8222f3d038c3714959c7c9b96cd2dee05: <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.12">2Ch 14:12</reference> <div eID="gen6018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6019" type="x-p"/> Asa, with his people, pursued to Gerar, the old ancient Philistine city, whose ruins Rowlands has discovered in the Khirbet el Gerar, in the Wady Jorf el Gerar (the torrent of Gerar), three leagues south-south-east of Gaza (see on <reference osisRef="Gen.20.1">Gen 20:1</reference>). “And there fell of the Cushites, so that to them was not revival,” i.e., so many that they could not make a stand and again collect themselves, <hi type="italic">ut eis vivificatio i. e. copias restaurandi ratio non esset, as older commentators,</hi> in <hi type="italic">Annott. uberior. ad h. l.,</hi> have already rightly interpreted it. The words are expressions for complete defeat. Berth. translates incorrectly: “until to them was nothing living;” for לאין does not stand for לאין עד, but ל serves to subordinate the clause, “so that no one,” where in the older language אין alone would have been sufficient, as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.25">2Ch 20:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.4">1Ch 22:4</reference>, cf. Ew. §315, <hi type="italic">c</hi>; and מחיה denotes, not “a living thing,” but only “preservation of life, vivification, revival, maintenance.” For they were broken before Jahve and before His host. מחנהוּ, i.e., Asa’s army is called Jahve’s, because Jahve fought in and with it against the enemy. There is no reason to suppose, with some older commentators, that there is any reference to an angelic host or heavenly camp (Gen 32:2.). And they (Asa and his people) brought back very much booty.
entries.12e605bd1d393cbc1185d3554bba56ad0db058b7: <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.13">2Ch 14:13</reference> “They smote all the cities round about Gerar,” which, as we must conclude from this, had made common cause with the Cushites, being inhabited by Philistines; for the fear of Jahve had fallen upon them. יהוה פּחד יהוה . here, and in <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.10">2Ch 17:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.29">2Ch 20:29</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.7">1Sa 11:7</reference>, the fear of the omnipotence displayed by Jahve in the annihilation of the innumerable hostile army. In these cities Judah found much booty.
entries.fa19098be3fc9dcfeeafb3765d252d1ee412cbfd: <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.14-2Chr.14.15">2Ch 14:14-15</reference> <div eID="gen6019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6020" type="x-p"/> They also smote the tents of the herds of the wandering tribes of that district, and carried away many sheep and camels as booty.  <chapter eID="2Chr.14"/> <div eID="gen6020" type="x-p"/>

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="14" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XIV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 SO Abijah slept with his fathers, and they bu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ried him in the city of David, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Kin, 15. 8<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> &c.</ns0:note> Asa his son reigned in his stead: in his days the land was quiet ten years <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> There was no open War, either by Baasha or others; onely there were secret Grudges and private Hostilities between his and Baasha's Subjects, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 15. 16.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And Asa did <ns0:hi>that which was</ns0:hi> good and right in the eyes of the LORD <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Of this and the next verse see on 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 15. 11, 12.</ns0:note> his God.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 For he took away the altars of the strange <ns0:hi>gods,</ns0:hi> and the high places, and brake down the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> statde<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> ima<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ges, and cut down the groves:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And commanded Judah to seek the LORD God of their fathers <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">By his Royal Edicts he required them to worship God, and him onely.</ns0:note>, and to do the law and the commandment <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To practise all which the Laws of Moses re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quired of them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Also he took away out of all the cities of Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dah the high places, and the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>sun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />images.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> images: and the king<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom was quiet before him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And he built fenced cities in Judah: for the land had rest, and he had no war in those years, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause the LORD had given him rest.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Therefore he said unto Judah, Let us build these cities, and make about <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> walls, and towers, gates, and bars, while the land <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> yet before us <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In out Power, as that Phrase is oft used. See on <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 13. 9.</ns0:note>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> because we have sought the LORD our God, we have sought <ns0:hi>him,</ns0:hi> and he hath given us rest on every side: so they built and prospered.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:349" />8 And Asa had an army <ns0:hi>of men</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which, as it seems, he had now gathered together upon the Information of Zerahs Design against him.</ns0:note>, that bare tar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gets and spears, out of Judah, three hundred thou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sand, and out of Benjamin, that bare sh<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>elds and drew bows, two hundred and fourscore thousand: all these <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> mighty men of valour.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 16. 3.</ns0:note> And there came out against them Zerah the Ethiopian <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>the Arabian<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                        </ns0:hi> as the Hebrew word <ns0:hi>Cush</ns0:hi> is commonly used, as hath been noted before: These being much nearer to Asa than the Ethiopians, who also could not have come to Asa but thorough Egypt, which probably the King of Egypt would not permit him to do.</ns0:note> with an host of a thousand thousand, and three hundred chariots, and came unto Mare<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sha <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">A City upon and within the Borders of Judah, <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 15. 44.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Then Asa went out against him, and they set the battel in aray in the valley of Zephathah, at Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />reshah.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And Asa cried unto the LORD his God, and said, LORD, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>it is not for <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> to help amongst many, him that hath no strength.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Sam. 14. 6.</ns0:note> nothing with thee <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e is no difference, or no difficulty, with thee.</ns0:note> to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power. Help us, O LORD our God, for we rest on thee, and in thy Name <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">By thy <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, in confidence of thy Assistance, and for the main<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tenance of thy Honour, and Service, and People.</ns0:note> we go against this mul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />titude. O LORD, thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> our God, let not <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>mortal man.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> man prevail against thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 So the LORD smote the Ethiopians before Asa, and before Judah, and the Ethiopians fled.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And Asa and the people that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him, pursued them unto Gerar <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">A City of the Philistins, who probably were Confederat<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> with them in this Design.</ns0:note>: and the Ethiopians were overthrown, that they could not recover them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves, for they were <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>broken.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> destroyed before the LORD, and before his host, and they carried away very much spoil.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And they smote all the cities round about Gerar <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Partly because they had joyned with Zerah in this War; and partly because the Ethiopians had sheltred a great part of the Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mains of the Army in them.</ns0:note>, for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 35. 5. Chap. 17. 10.</ns0:note> the fear of the LORD came upon them: and they spoiled all the cities, for there was exceeding much spoil in them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 They smote also the tents of cattel <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The dwellers in Tents, which were either a Part of Ze<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rahs Company, or joyned with them, or had come along with them to furnish that Great Host with necessary Provisions; which their Custom of dwelling in Tents made them more capable of doing.</ns0:note>, and carried away sheep and camels in abundance, and re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />turned to Jerusalem.</ns0:p>
